note: "Diabolisation" keeps British spelling; the style note requires American.
replacement: 21. So much for my rough, preliminary sketch of how the ideas "ought" (owe) and "duty" are interrelated with the postulates of religion. Until now I have intentionally held back the actual moralization of these ideas (their being pushed back into the conscience, or more precisely the interweaving of the bad conscience with the idea of God). At the end of the last paragraph I spoke as if this moralization did not exist, and as if these ideas had therefore necessarily come to an end, since their hypothesis, the belief in our "creditor," in God, had collapsed. The actual facts differ terribly from this theory. With the moralization of the ideas "ought" and "duty," and their being pushed back into the bad conscience, comes the first actual attempt to reverse the direction of the development we have just described, or at any rate to arrest its progress. It is just at this juncture that the very hope of an eventual redemption has to shut itself once for all in the prison of pessimism; it is at this juncture that the eye has to recoil and rebound in despair from an adamantine impossibility; it is at this juncture that the ideas "guilt" and "duty" have to turn backwards. Turn backwards against whom? There is no doubt about it: primarily against the "ower." In him the bad conscience now establishes itself, eats, spreads and grows like a polypus throughout his length and breadth, and with such virulence that at last, with the impossibility of paying the debt, there is conceived the impossibility of paying the penalty, the thought of its inexpiability (the idea of "eternal punishment"). Finally it also turns against the "creditor." It may find him in the causa prima of man, the origin of the human race, its sire, who from then on is burdened with a curse ("Adam," "original sin," "determination of the will"). Or it may find him in Nature, from whose womb man springs, and on whom the responsibility for the principle of evil is now cast ("Diabolization of Nature"). Or it may find him in existence generally, which on this logic is an absolute white elephant, with which mankind is landed (the Nihilistic flight from life, the demand for Nothingness, or for the opposite of existence, for some other existence, Buddhism and the like). Then suddenly we stand before that paradoxical and awful expedient through which a tortured humanity found a temporary alleviation, that stroke of genius called Christianity: God personally sacrificing himself for the debt of man, God paying himself personally out of a pound of his own flesh, God as the one being who can deliver man from what man had become unable to deliver himself from — the creditor playing scapegoat for his debtor, from love (can you believe it?), from love of his debtor!...

note: Source parenthetical aside "(to him incomprehensible)" was dissolved into a clause.
replacement: Yet note that this Olympian spectator and judge is not at all angry with them, and does not think ill of them for it. "How foolish they are," he thinks of the misdeeds of mortals. And "folly," "imprudence," "a little brain disturbance," and nothing more, are what the Greeks, even of the strongest, bravest period, have admitted to be the ground of much that is evil and fatal. — Folly, not sin, do you understand?... But even this brain disturbance was a problem. "Come, how is it even possible? How could it really have got into brains like ours, the brains of men of aristocratic ancestry, of men of fortune, of men of good natural endowments, of men of the best society, of men of nobility and virtue?" This was the question the aristocratic Greek asked himself for century after century, whenever he was confronted with every (to him incomprehensible) outrage and sacrilege with which one of his peers had polluted himself. "It must be that a god had infatuated him," he would say at last, nodding his head. — This solution is typical of the Greeks, ... and accordingly the gods in those times served to justify man to a certain extent even in evil. In those days they took upon themselves not the punishment but, what is more noble, the guilt.
